title: 🎯 Welcome to Lexical Resource — Your 25% Score

sections.heading: What is Lexical Resource?
sections.body:
Lexical Resource (LR) is one of four equally weighted criteria in IELTS Writing and Speaking — it accounts for 25% of your total score.

LR does NOT simply measure how many rare words you know. It measures:
• The RANGE of vocabulary you use
• How ACCURATELY you use it
• How NATURALLY it fits the context
• Whether you can express PRECISE meaning

A Band 5 student knows 500 words. A Band 9 student knows the same words — but also knows how to use them with flexibility and precision.

sections.heading: What this lesson covers
sections.body:
This lesson introduces six high-value academic words that appear repeatedly in IELTS essays and academic texts:

1. mitigate — reduce severity
2. exacerbate — make worse
3. ubiquitous — found everywhere
4. proliferate — increase rapidly
5. substantiate — prove with evidence
6. alleviate — relieve or reduce

For each word, you will learn: meaning, pronunciation, collocations, word family, common errors, and how to use it in exam conditions.

highlight: One precise word used correctly outweighs five vague ones. This lesson trains precision, not just quantity.

title: 📊 The Band Score Ladder for Lexical Resource

sections.heading: What each band looks like
sections.body:
Band 5: Uses basic vocabulary with limited range. Errors in spelling and word choice are frequent. Repetition is obvious.

Band 6: Attempts less common words, but errors occur. Uses some collocations but not always naturally. Some paraphrasing.

Band 7: Uses a sufficient range with some less common items. Occasional inaccuracies but meaning is clear. Collocations are generally correct.

Band 8: Wide range used with flexibility. Minor inaccuracies only. Precise meaning conveyed. Natural collocations throughout.

Band 9: Full flexibility and precise meaning. Rare and sophisticated items used naturally. Zero or near-zero errors.

sections.heading: The single biggest mistake at Band 6
sections.body:
Band 6 writers tend to:
• Use the same word 3–4 times in one essay (e.g., 'important', 'problem', 'big')
• Use informal words like 'a lot', 'really', 'thing', 'stuff'
• Use advanced words incorrectly — which is WORSE than using simple words correctly

The rule: Only use a word if you are confident in its EXACT meaning and collocations.

example.wrong: Technology is a very important thing. It has caused many problems and many people use it a lot in their lives today.
example.right: Technology has become ubiquitous in modern life, proliferating across every sector and fundamentally reshaping how individuals work, communicate, and access information.

title: 🗺️ How to Use This Lesson
body:
Each word is introduced with:
✅ A flashcard — meaning, example, common error
✅ Practice questions — MCQs, fill-in-the-blanks, reordering
✅ Mini-explainers — comparisons with similar words

Tip: Don't just read the correct answer. Read every WRONG answer and understand WHY it is wrong. This trains your instinct for precision.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to use all six words in an IELTS essay without hesitation.

quick.label: Check the collocations — which words go with it?
Learn the word family (noun, verb, adjective)
Spot errors — this trains exam instinct

meaning: to reduce the severity, seriousness, or painfulness of something
example: International cooperation is essential to mitigate the long-term effects of climate change.
wrong: Do NOT confuse with 'exacerbate' (to make worse). They are direct opposites.
family: unmitigated (adj) — 'an unmitigated disaster' (= total, with nothing to reduce it)

title: ⚖️ mitigate vs exacerbate — The Most Tested Pair
body:
These two verbs are among the most commonly confused in IELTS Writing. They are direct antonyms:

✅ MITIGATE = make LESS severe
'Urban trees mitigate the effects of air pollution.'
(Trees reduce the pollution problem)

❌ EXACERBATE = make MORE severe
'Deforestation exacerbates the effects of air pollution.'
(Deforestation makes the problem worse)

Memory trick:
MITIgate → think of 'MITI-gate' = a gate that BLOCKS and REDUCES something
EXACERbate → think of 'EX-ACER-bate' = EXCEED + ACERBIC (sharp/harsh) = make sharper, worse

question: Which sentence uses 'mitigate' correctly?
options: Poverty has mitigated educational inequality across the region.
Governments can mitigate the effects of flooding by investing in drainage infrastructure.
The new law will mitigate crime rates and make things worse.
Stress is known to mitigate a range of serious health conditions.
correct: Governments can mitigate the effects of flooding by investing in drainage infrastructure.
explanation:
✅ 'Mitigate the effects of flooding' — investment reduces (lessens) the flood damage. Perfect usage.

❌ 'Poverty has mitigated educational inequality' — poverty makes inequality WORSE (exacerbates), not better.
❌ 'Make things worse' contradicts mitigate — the sentence is self-contradictory.
❌ 'Stress mitigates health conditions' — stress WORSENS conditions; 'exacerbates' is correct here.
hint: Mitigate always makes something LESS harmful or severe — never worse.

sentence: Early medical intervention can significantly _______ the severity of symptoms in patients with chronic conditions.
explanation:
'Mitigate the severity' = reduce how severe the symptoms are. Medical intervention REDUCES, not worsens, symptoms.

❌ 'Exacerbate' — this would mean intervention makes symptoms WORSE
❌ 'Proliferate' — this is intransitive and means 'to multiply'; it doesn't fit here
❌ 'Substantiate' — means to prove with evidence; doesn't fit symptom severity
hint: Does medical intervention make symptoms better or worse?

meaning: to make a bad situation, problem, or feeling worse
example: Rapid urbanisation has exacerbated existing inequalities between wealthy and low-income communities.
wrong: NOT the same as 'cause'. Exacerbate means to WORSEN something that already exists — it cannot create a new problem from nothing.

question: Which sentence uses 'exacerbate' correctly?
options: Social media has exacerbated a new kind of loneliness that never existed before.
The government's austerity policies exacerbated pre-existing poverty among the most vulnerable.
Regular exercise can exacerbate mental and physical health outcomes.
Education has been shown to exacerbate social mobility over time.
correct: The government's austerity policies exacerbated pre-existing poverty among the most vulnerable.
explanation:
✅ 'Exacerbated pre-existing poverty' — the poverty already existed; austerity made it WORSE. 'Pre-existing' even reinforces the correct use.

❌ 'A new kind of loneliness that never existed before' — exacerbate cannot CREATE something new; only worsen what exists
❌ 'Exercise exacerbates health outcomes' — exercise IMPROVES health; 'enhances' or 'improves' is correct
❌ 'Education exacerbates social mobility' — education increases social mobility; 'exacerbate' implies worsening
hint: Exacerbate requires something that already exists and is being made worse.

sentence: A lack of affordable housing _______ the challenges faced by low-income families in urban areas.
explanation:
'Exacerbates the challenges' = makes the challenges worse. Low-income families already face challenges; lack of housing makes those challenges harder.

❌ 'Mitigates' and 'Alleviates' both mean to REDUCE challenges — the opposite of what makes sense here.
❌ 'Substantiates' = proves with evidence — grammatically and semantically incorrect here.
hint: Does lack of affordable housing make the challenges better or worse?

meaning: present, appearing, or found everywhere, often to a notable degree
example: Personal data collection has become ubiquitous in the digital economy, raising profound questions about privacy.
wrong: NOT the same as 'common' or 'popular'. Ubiquitous implies something is EVERYWHERE — so prevalent it is almost unavoidable.

instruction: Arrange the words to form a correct academic sentence:
correct: Digital surveillance technology has become ubiquitous in the modern era.
explanation:
Structure: Subject (Digital surveillance technology) + auxiliary verb (has) + main verb (become) + adjective (ubiquitous) + prepositional phrase (in the modern era).

Key grammar points:
• 'Has become' — present perfect (started in past, true now)
• 'Ubiquitous' follows 'become' as a predicative adjective
• 'In the modern era' — prepositional phrase at the end adds academic formality

meaning: to increase rapidly and spread to many places; to multiply in great numbers
example: Misinformation has proliferated at an alarming rate across digital platforms in recent years.
wrong: Proliferate is INTRANSITIVE — it does not take a direct object. You CANNOT say 'proliferate something'. Say 'X proliferates' or 'X has proliferated'.
collocations: proliferate rapidly / at an alarming rate

question: Which sentence uses 'proliferate' or 'proliferation' most accurately?
options: The government proliferated new policies to address the crisis.
The proliferation of ride-sharing apps has fundamentally disrupted the traditional taxi industry.
Scientists have successfully proliferated a cure for the disease.
Social media apps proliferate young people's attention spans.
correct: The proliferation of ride-sharing apps has fundamentally disrupted the traditional taxi industry.
explanation:
✅ 'The proliferation of ride-sharing apps' — apps have increased rapidly in number (noun form used correctly as subject).

❌ 'The government proliferated new policies' — proliferate is intransitive; you cannot proliferate SOMETHING
❌ 'Proliferated a cure' — same error; proliferate takes no object
❌ 'Proliferate young people's attention spans' — again transitive misuse; attention spans don't proliferate
hint: Remember: proliferate is intransitive. Things proliferate — you cannot proliferate something.

meaning: to provide evidence to support, verify, or prove a claim or argument
example: The researcher substantiated her hypothesis with three independent longitudinal studies.
wrong: NOT the same as 'cause' or 'create'. Substantiate is about EVIDENCE and PROOF — not about making something happen.

title: ✏️ Spot the Vocabulary Error
instruction: One of these sentences misuses 'substantiate'. Which one?

sentences.text: The committee demanded that all claims be substantiated with peer-reviewed research before publication.
Industrial pollution has substantiated the decline in biodiversity across the northern wetlands.
sentences.explanation:
'Substantiate' means to PROVE or PROVIDE EVIDENCE for something — not to cause or worsen it.

✅ Correct version: 'Industrial pollution has exacerbated the decline in biodiversity across the northern wetlands.'

This is a Band 6–7 error: using a sophisticated word without knowing its precise meaning. The examiner will penalise this more severely than using a simpler word correctly.

sentences.text: Without data to substantiate the hypothesis, the argument remains unconvincing.

meaning: to make suffering, pain, or a difficult situation less severe; to provide partial relief
example: Urban green spaces can help alleviate stress and improve the mental health of city residents.
wrong: Alleviate means to PARTIALLY reduce — not to eliminate. 'Alleviate poverty' means reduce its burden, not end it completely. For complete removal, use 'eradicate' or 'eliminate'.

question: Which word best completes this sentence? 'Investment in public transport could _______ traffic congestion in major cities.'
options: exacerbate
proliferate
alleviate
substantiate
explanation:
✅ 'Alleviate traffic congestion' — public transport reduces (partially relieves) the burden of congestion.

❌ 'Exacerbate' — this would mean transport WORSENS congestion
❌ 'Proliferate' — this is intransitive and means things increase in number; doesn't fit grammatically
❌ 'Substantiate' — means to prove with evidence; not relevant to traffic problems
hint: We want a verb meaning 'reduce or ease the problem of congestion'.

sentence: International aid programmes are designed to _______ the immediate suffering caused by natural disasters, though they cannot address the underlying structural causes.
explanation:
'Alleviate immediate suffering' is the most natural collocation here. The context confirms partial relief ('cannot address underlying causes'), which aligns with alleviate's meaning of partial reduction.

'Mitigate' is also possible but 'alleviate suffering' is a much stronger, more natural collocation than 'mitigate suffering'. In IELTS, choosing the most natural collocation is rewarded.

❌ 'Substantiate' — proves claims; irrelevant to suffering
❌ 'Exacerbate' — makes worse; opposite of what aid programmes do
hint: Think about what international aid actually does to suffering — reduce it or worsen it?

instruction: Match each word to its precise academic meaning:

pairs.meaning: reduce the severity or seriousness of a negative situation
make an existing problem or bad situation significantly worse
present and found virtually everywhere in a given context
increase rapidly in number and spread across a wide area
support or verify a claim by providing concrete evidence

explanation:
These five words form a core academic cluster that appears across IELTS essays on nearly every topic — technology, environment, society, health, education.

Note how they differ subtly:
• Mitigate and alleviate both reduce something — but mitigate often relates to damage/impact; alleviate to suffering/burden
• Exacerbate always requires a pre-existing problem
• Substantiate is specifically about evidence and argument — not causation

title: 🌳 Word Families — Double Your Vocabulary Instantly

sections.heading: Why word families matter
sections.body:
Knowing a word's FAMILY means you can use it as a noun, verb, and adjective — which allows you to vary your sentence structure and avoid repetition.

mitigate (v) → mitigation (n) → mitigating (adj)
exacerbate (v) → exacerbation (n)
ubiquitous (adj) → ubiquity (n)
proliferate (v) → proliferation (n)
substantiate (v) → substantiation (n) → substantiated / unsubstantiated (adj)
alleviate (v) → alleviation (n)

sections.heading: Using them in essays
sections.body:
Using the noun form allows you to vary your sentence openings:

❌ Repetitive: 'Technology has proliferated. This proliferation has caused problems.'

✅ Varied: 'The proliferation of mobile devices across emerging economies presents both opportunities and risks.'

Note: 'The proliferation of X' (noun + of) is a particularly useful sentence-opening structure for Task 2 introductions.

highlight: For every verb you learn, immediately learn its noun form. This doubles your writing flexibility with zero extra effort.

title: ✍️ Using These Words in IELTS Task 2

sections.heading: In your introduction (paraphrase + thesis)
sections.body:
Avoid: 'Social media is everywhere and it causes many problems.'

Better: 'The ubiquity of social media platforms, which have proliferated at an unprecedented rate, has fundamentally altered human communication — though critics argue these developments exacerbate existing social inequalities rather than mitigate them.'

sections.heading: In body paragraphs (argument + evidence)
sections.body:
Avoid: 'There is some proof that exercise helps mental health.'

Better: 'Substantial clinical evidence substantiates the link between regular physical activity and improved psychological wellbeing, suggesting that urban planning policies should prioritise accessible exercise facilities as a means of alleviating the burden of mental health disorders.'

sections.heading: In your conclusion (summary + implication)
sections.body:
Avoid: 'In conclusion, there are many problems and we need to solve them.'

Better: 'In conclusion, while technology has undeniably exacerbated certain social problems, well-designed regulatory frameworks offer a viable pathway to mitigate these harms and ensure that the benefits of digital innovation are equitably distributed.'

highlight: Notice how each model sentence uses multiple target words naturally — not forced, not random. This is what Band 8+ looks like.

question: Which sentence represents the best Band 8 use of academic vocabulary?
options: Climate change is a very big problem and governments need to do something to make it less bad.
Climate change is an important issue that is getting worse, and governments must mitigate it.
The proliferation of carbon-intensive industries has significantly exacerbated climate instability, underscoring the urgent need for substantiated policy responses.
Carbon emissions have increased a lot and this has made climate change worse so we need policies.
correct: The proliferation of carbon-intensive industries has significantly exacerbated climate instability, underscoring the urgent need for substantiated policy responses.
explanation:
✅ Band 8+ features:
• 'proliferation of' — sophisticated noun phrase
• 'exacerbated climate instability' — precise verb + academic noun
• 'underscoring the urgent need' — sophisticated participle clause
• 'substantiated policy responses' — adjective form used precisely
• Zero vague words (no 'very', 'a lot', 'big', 'bad')

❌ Options A and D are Band 5–6: informal, vague, repetitive
❌ Option B is Band 6–7: uses 'mitigate' but 'mitigate climate change' is imprecise ('mitigate the effects of' is more accurate)
hint: Look for precise nouns, strong verbs, and zero vague intensifiers.

title: ✏️ Advanced Error Detection
instruction: One sentence contains a sophisticated vocabulary error. Identify it.

sentences.text: The alleviation of extreme poverty requires sustained investment in education and infrastructure.
The new stadium proliferated a sense of civic pride throughout the city.
sentences.explanation:
'Proliferate' is INTRANSITIVE — it cannot take an object. You cannot 'proliferate a sense of something'.

✅ Correct option A: 'The new stadium engendered a sense of civic pride throughout the city.'
✅ Correct option B: 'A sense of civic pride proliferated throughout the city following the stadium's opening.'

This is a Band 7–8 level error — the candidate knows the word but misunderstands its grammar. Examiners catch this.

sentences.text: Unsubstantiated claims about vaccine safety have exacerbated public mistrust in medical institutions.

question: Which sentence most precisely distinguishes 'mitigate' from 'alleviate'?
options: Both words mean the same thing and can always be used interchangeably.
'Alleviate' specifically refers to suffering or burden, while 'mitigate' more broadly describes reducing any negative impact, risk, or severity.
'Mitigate' is informal; 'alleviate' is the academic preference.
'Alleviate' means to completely remove, while 'mitigate' only partially reduces.
correct: 'Alleviate' specifically refers to suffering or burden, while 'mitigate' more broadly describes reducing any negative impact, risk, or severity.
explanation:
✅ This is the most accurate description of the distinction:
• 'Alleviate poverty / pain / suffering / pressure / burden' — collocation is with human hardship
• 'Mitigate risk / impact / damage / effects / consequences' — broader, often environmental or systemic

❌ They are NOT interchangeable — 'mitigate suffering' sounds unnatural; 'alleviate risk' is awkward
❌ Neither word implies COMPLETE removal — that's 'eradicate' or 'eliminate'
❌ Both are equally formal in academic writing
hint: Think about what typically follows each word as its object.

title: 🏁 Lesson Summary — Academic Words Set 1

sections.heading: Words mastered in this lesson
sections.body:
✅ mitigate — reduce severity or harmful effects
✅ exacerbate — worsen an existing problem (always pre-existing)
✅ ubiquitous — found everywhere, highly prevalent
✅ proliferate — increase rapidly in number (INTRANSITIVE)
✅ substantiate — prove with evidence (about claims, not causes)
✅ alleviate — reduce suffering, burden, or pressure (partial relief)

sections.heading: Key distinctions to remember
sections.body:
mitigate vs exacerbate → opposites (reduce vs worsen)
mitigate vs alleviate → similar, but alleviate = human suffering/burden
substantiate vs cause → completely different (proof vs creation)
proliferate → always intransitive; cannot take a direct object

Examiner's perspective: Using these words incorrectly is worse than not using them at all. Confident, accurate use of simpler words always beats uncertain use of complex ones.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.body:
Academic Words Set 2 introduces six more high-value verbs:
precipitate, engender, underpin, undermine, disproportionate, contend

These focus on causation, support, and academic stance — the building blocks of sophisticated IELTS arguments.

highlight: Review these six words every day for one week. Use each in one sentence from your own life. That's how they move from 'recognised' to 'owned'.
